---
title: "1. Mapping crt K76T in the Greater Horn of Africa"
description: >
  From a STAVE data object to monthly maps, country trends and probability
  statements: the chloroquine-resistance marker crt K76T across the eight
  IGAD countries, 1989-2024.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110,
                      out.width = "100%")
library(ggplot2)
# site builds: GADM files downloaded earlier, if STAREAL_GADM_CACHE names a folder of them
local({
  cache <- Sys.getenv("STAREAL_GADM_CACHE")
  if (nzchar(cache)) {
    dir.create(file.path(tempdir(), "gadm"), showWarnings = FALSE)
    file.copy(list.files(cache, pattern = "^gadm41_", full.names = TRUE), file.path(tempdir(), "gadm"))
  }
})
```

The *Plasmodium falciparum* crt K76T mutation is the main marker of
chloroquine resistance. Chloroquine was replaced as the first-line treatment
for falciparum malaria across East Africa between the late 1990s and the
mid-2000s, and where it stopped being used the resistant parasites lost
their advantage. This tutorial maps K76T month by month across the eight
member states of IGAD (Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, South
Sudan, Sudan and Uganda) from 1989 to 2024, and asks:

- how prevalence changed in each country, with honest uncertainty;
- where the chloroquine-sensitive parasite is now dominant;
- where the data are too thin to say.

```{r packages}
library(stareal)
```

## 1. The data: a STAVE object

STAVE stores studies, surveys and variant counts. The public data set is an
R object of a little over 250 kB; reading it needs the
[STAVE package](https://github.com/mrc-ide/STAVE).

```{r stave}
url <- paste0("https://github.com/IDEELResearch/scrub/raw/2d85d021efe1c93dc55300610d944c9fbaf4af1a/",
              "analysis/data-out/stave_data_2026.03.17.rds")
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
download.file(url, tmp, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
stave <- suppressWarnings(readRDS(tmp))
stave
```

The prevalence of a variant comes from `get_prevalence()`. It counts every
survey that genotyped the codon, whatever format the study used, including
the surveys where the mutant was absent. Setting `return_full = FALSE` drops any rows where the *denominator* is zero, which is what we want here:

```{r prevalence}
p <- stave$get_prevalence("crt:76:T", return_full = FALSE)
nrow(p)
```

These are the surveys of every country in the data set. Section 3 selects
those in the region of interest.

## 2. The spatial frame

The areas are the first-level administrative units of the eight countries,
from [GADM](https://gadm.org) version 4.1, downloaded with the
[geodata](https://cran.r-project.org/package=geodata) package. GADM's
licence allows free academic and other non-commercial use but not
redistribution, so the boundaries are downloaded rather than shipped with
*stareal*. The low-resolution files (`resolution = 2`) are ample for maps
at this scale.

```{r gadm}
iso3 <- c("DJI", "ERI", "ETH", "KEN", "SOM", "SSD", "SDN", "UGA")
adm1 <- sf::st_as_sf(geodata::gadm(iso3, level = 1, path = tempdir(), version = "4.1", resolution = 2))
table(adm1$COUNTRY)
```

Uganda's first level in GADM is its districts, so it has many more units
than its neighbours.

**Lakes are not places where people live**, and GADM treats them
inconsistently. Uganda's parts of Lakes Victoria and Albert are units of
their own, while Kenya's and Ethiopia's lakes are folded into the
surrounding units. Left in, a lake would get a prevalence of its own, or
stretch a lakeside unit across the water and make it a neighbour of units
on the far shore. So the large lakes are cut out of every unit, using the
public-domain lakes of [Natural Earth](https://www.naturalearthdata.com),
downloaded with the
[rnaturalearth](https://cran.r-project.org/package=rnaturalearth) package.
The cutting is done in an equal-area projection centred on the region,
which the frame then keeps for its distances. Note that this step is simply a
quirk of us using GADM 4.1 shapefiles - if you use your own shapefile then this
should hopefully not be needed.

```{r lakes, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}
lakes <- rnaturalearth::ne_download(scale = 10, type = "lakes", category = "physical",
                                    returnclass = "sf", destdir = tempdir())
crs <- "+proj=laea +lat_0=8 +lon_0=37 +units=m"          # equal-area, centred on the region
adm1 <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_transform(adm1, crs))
lakes <- sf::st_make_valid(sf::st_transform(lakes, crs))
lakes <- lakes[as.numeric(sf::st_area(lakes)) > 1e9, ]  # lakes over 1,000 km2
water <- sf::st_intersection(sf::st_union(lakes), sf::st_union(adm1))
adm1 <- sf::st_difference(adm1, water)
adm1 <- adm1[adm1$ENGTYPE_1 != "Water body", ]           # what is left of Uganda's lake units
```

Now we have a nice clean shapefile
```{r}
class(adm1)
dim(adm1)
```

`areal_frame()` converts a shapefile into the elements needed by the model. 
It finds the neighbours of every unit, links any islands to
the nearest unit of the same country, and computes the eigendecomposition
of the graph that the model needs. That is a one-off step, quick for a few
hundred units. With thousands of units, build the frame once and save it
with `saveRDS()`.

```{r frame}
fr <- areal_frame(adm1, id = "GID_1", groups = c(country = "COUNTRY"),
                  link_within = "country", verbose = FALSE)
fr
```

We can visualize the adjacency graph between areas:

```{r frame-plot, fig.height = 6}
plot(fr)
```

## 3. The surveys in the region

STAVE treats a survey’s coordinates, not its country name, as the authoritative record of where it took place. Country names are stored as free text making them inherently unstable - they vary in spelling, case, special characters, and may be prone to mistakes. Latitude and longitude are the fields intended for spatial selection, surveys are therefore selected by location: those within 10 km of one of the units. Distances are measured in the frame's planar projection, `fr$crs_planar`. This is the same rule that `areal_data()` uses to assign a point just outside every
polygon, such as a coastal site, to the nearest unit.

```{r select}
pts <- sf::st_transform(sf::st_as_sf(p, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326), fr$crs_planar)
units <- sf::st_transform(adm1, fr$crs_planar)
surveys <- p[lengths(sf::st_is_within_distance(pts, units, dist = 10000)) > 0, ]
nrow(surveys)
```

These are exactly the surveys in `igad_crt76t`, the example data that ship
with *stareal*:

```{r same-as-packaged}
all.equal(sort(surveys$survey_id), sort(igad_crt76t$survey_id))
```

## 4. Time, and the survey data

We want to draw inference in monthly steps from 1989 to 2024:

```{r time}
tf <- time_frame(1989, 2024, "month")
tf
```

`areal_data()` puts each survey in a unit and a month, and pools surveys in
the same unit and month. A survey's month is that of its `collection_day`:
the middle of its collection window, or the date the study gave. This is where the areal frame, the time frame, and the survey data come together.

```{r data}
d <- areal_data(surveys, fr, tf, y = "numerator", k = "denominator",
                coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), date = "collection_day")
d
```

We can produce a simple plot to see how data are distributed in space and time:

```{r data-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(d)
```

The data are clumped in both space and time. Only `r nrow(d$cells)` of the
`r format(fr$m * tf$n_steps, big.mark = ",")` unit-months have data. The
model fills the gaps from neighbouring units and months, and presents uncertainty as part of the answer.

## 5. Fitting

The defaults run four chains of 3,000 iterations, in parallel. This example should take no more than a couple of minutes on a modern laptop:

```{r fit, message = FALSE}
fit <- fit_areal(d)
```

`diagnose()` checks the R-hat and effective sample size (ESS) of every
parameter, including the latent prevalence of every observed cell. We want small R-hat, indicating the MCMC has converged, but large ESS, indicating it has adequately explored the posterior:

```{r diagnose}
diagnose(fit)
```

Every check passes. That is not guaranteed: sparse or mostly-zero data mix
more slowly (see [tutorial 2](k13-561h.html)). A `summary()` of the fit shows some more detail including parameter estimates, and a `plot()` gives a visual check of the MCMC behaviour:

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

```{r traces, fig.height = 6}
plot(fit)
```

This is good enough for our preliminary analysis. For publishable results, a longer run gives more draws in the tails of the intervals - particularly important when calculating exceedance probabilities. With `checkpoint_dir` set, an
interrupted run picks up where it stopped when the same call is run again (note, this line will take longer to run - skip if you just want preliminary results):

```{r long, eval = FALSE}
fit <- fit_areal(d, control = list(n_iter = 20000, n_burn = 5000, n_store = 250, theta_thin = 10),
                 checkpoint_dir = "chains/crt76t")
```

How to read the parameters:

- `sigma` sets the size of the variation around the trend, on the logit
  scale.
- `rho_s` close to 1 means neighbouring units are strongly alike.
- `rho_t` is the correlation from one month to the next. Close to 1, as
  here, prevalence changes slowly.
- `sigma_n` is the scatter between unit-months, beyond what the field
  explains (different sites, sampling, methods).
- `intercept` is the logit prevalence at the middle of the window, before
  the field.
- `trend` is half the change in logit prevalence over the window, before
  the field. A strongly negative value is the regional decline.

## 6. Predicting the full surface

`predict()` reconstructs the prevalence of every unit in every month, once
per posterior draw, and aggregates each draw to the countries. Country
estimates here are unweighted means over their units; with population or
parasite-burden data you can give them as `weights`.

```{r predict, message = FALSE}
pr <- predict(fit, groups = "country", exceedance = 5)
pr
```

Maps for three months, made with `sf::st_as_sf()`, which joins one month's
estimates to the polygons, with the lakes cut out earlier drawn as water:

```{r maps, fig.height = 4}
months <- c("2000-07", "2010-07", "2024-07")
m <- do.call(rbind, lapply(months, function(t) sf::st_as_sf(pr, time = t)))
ggplot(m) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = mean), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = sf::st_sf(water), fill = "#bcd6ea", colour = NA) +
  facet_wrap(~time) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("K76T\nprevalence (%)", limits = c(0, 100), option = "magma") +
  theme_void()
```

We can also look at trends over time. The next plot gives country trends, with the 95% interval as a shaded ribbon, and the data overlaid for comparison (exact 95% binomial interval from raw survey data). The data are from surveyed units only,
while the band covers the whole country, so the two need not agree where
few units are surveyed.

```{r countries, fig.height = 6}
plot(pr, group = "country", ids = c("Kenya", "Uganda", "Sudan", "Ethiopia", "South Sudan", "Somalia"))
```

Kenya and Uganda tell the clearest story. K76T was common, above 80%,
until the late 2000s, then fell, to around 10% by 2024. Sudan's decline is
slower and less certain. Ethiopia is different: its surveys up to 2022
still find K76T in most infections. Ethiopia still treats *P. vivax*
malaria with chloroquine, a likely reason. After its last surveys, the
country's band drifts down with the trend of the region as a whole. The
model has one trend for all eight countries, so it extrapolates the
region's decline into a country that may not share it.
[Tutorial 3](covariates.html) gives countries trends of their own. In
Somalia, with two surveys, and South Sudan, with six and none since 2014,
the estimates lean on the neighbours and the regional trend, and the bands
are wide.

We can also dig into the trends within sub-national regions. For example, the next plot shows trends for all 11 tier-one subdivisions of Ethiopia:

```{r country-table}
ids <- sprintf("ETH.%s_1", 1:11)
plot(pr, ids = ids, labels = adm1$NAME_1[match(ids, adm1$GID_1)])
```

We see very different trends in the West (e.g. Gambela) compared with the East (e.g. Oromia).

## 7. Probability statements, and where the data run out

The posterior answers questions directly. Where is K76T still above 5%?
`predict()` was asked for that probability with `exceedance = 5` (in
percent, like every prevalence in *stareal*), and reports it as `p_gt_5`:

```{r prob-above, fig.height = 4.5}
m24 <- sf::st_as_sf(pr, time = "2024-07")
ggplot(m24) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = p_gt_5), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = sf::st_sf(water), fill = "#bcd6ea", colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("P(prevalence\n> 5%),\nJuly 2024", limits = c(0, 1), option = "magma") +
  theme_void()
```

The units by how sure the model is, country by country: probably above 5%
(a probability over 0.9), probably below (under 0.1), or uncertain:

```{r prob-above-table}
m24$call <- cut(m24$p_gt_5, c(0, 0.1, 0.9, 1), include.lowest = TRUE,
                labels = c("probably below", "uncertain", "probably above"))
table(m24$country, m24$call)
```

K76T is probably still above 5% across the Horn: in most units of
Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia and Djibouti. Ethiopia's recent surveys find it
common, and its neighbours, with few or no surveys of their own, borrow
from them. In Kenya and Uganda, where it fell furthest, most units are
uncertain. Their prevalence, around 5 to 10%, sits close to the threshold,
and only `r sum(m24$call == "probably below")` units in the whole region
are probably below it. A low threshold is a demanding question: saying
with confidence that prevalence is below 5% takes many recent surveys
that find little.

Uncertainty is not uniform. The posterior standard deviation in July 2024,
beside the total number tested in each unit over the whole period:

```{r uncertainty, fig.height = 4}
m24$tested <- tapply(pr$area$k, pr$area$id, sum)[m24$id]
m24$tested[m24$tested == 0] <- NA
g1 <- ggplot(m24) + geom_sf(aes(fill = sd), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = sf::st_sf(water), fill = "#bcd6ea", colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("posterior sd\n(% points),\nJuly 2024", option = "magma") + theme_void()
g2 <- ggplot(m24) + geom_sf(aes(fill = tested), colour = "grey85", linewidth = 0.05) +
  geom_sf(data = sf::st_sf(water), fill = "#bcd6ea", colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("tested,\n1989-2024", trans = "log10", na.value = "grey95", option = "magma") +
  theme_void()
patchwork::wrap_plots(g1, g2)
```

The median standard deviation by country:

```{r sd-by-country}
round(tapply(m24$sd, m24$country, median), 2)
```

```{r sd-values, include = FALSE}
sd_med <- round(tapply(m24$sd, m24$country, median), 2)
```

Where there are few or no surveys, as in Djibouti, Eritrea, Somalia and
much of Sudan, the median standard deviation is about 30 percentage points, against
`r round(sd_med[["Uganda"]])` in Uganda and `r round(sd_med[["Kenya"]])` in Kenya. A map of the posterior mean alone would hide
this.

## 8. Taking the results away

The tables are ordinary data frames, and the maps ordinary `sf` objects:

```{r export, eval = FALSE}
write.csv(pr$area, "crt76t_by_unit_month.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(pr$groups$country, "crt76t_by_country_month.csv", row.names = FALSE)
sf::st_write(sf::st_as_sf(pr, time = "2024-07"), "crt76t_2024-07.gpkg")
```

The posterior draws of the parameters and of every observed cell are
available for your own summaries with `posterior::as_draws_df(fit)`.
